item.text: {"question_id":"4B.6","answer":"In 2023, the DRC maintained some formal access and oversight mechanisms, but the information environment remained materially pressured and did not reliably enable independent information. The revised press law guaranteed access to non-classified information of public interest and followed a national media convention, but tightened journalist accreditation and retained prison sentences for press offenses; the Digital Code imposed prison penalties for disseminating information deemed false. [BATCH-0025-E007, BATCH-0011-E011] The government did not restrict internet access or censor online content, and authorities initially invited a substantial EU election-observation mission, although it was later reduced to an eight-person expert mission operating from Kinshasa; the reason and eventual findings are unresolved. [BATCH-0011-E011, BATCH-0028-E007, BATCH-0028-E003] CENI also formally planned a mixed international-national audit with publication of results, but its completion and corrective effect are not established in the supplied record. [BATCH-0027-E011, BATCH-0023-E015] Against these qualifications, RSF described a non-independent national broadcaster, politician and local-authority pressure, opaque state media funding, limited independent viability, self-censorship, arrests, threats, disappearances, attacks, and impunity. [BATCH-0025-E007, BATCH-0025-E008] The 2023 record includes Bujakera’s detention and prosecution under provisions criminalizing information deemed false even though the report at issue did not name him as author; soldiers arrested and beat three journalists; at least seven journalists were assaulted in July election-related incidents, including an alleged assault by the leader and militants of an allied MLC party; and campaign-period journalists faced attacks, threats, and denial of access to public places and airports. [BATCH-0025-E012, BATCH-0026-E007, BATCH-0027-E004, BATCH-0027-E005, BATCH-0002-E025, BATCH-0002-E027] During the election period, alleged UDPS supporters attacked journalist Pascal Mulegwa, AREP supporters attacked Réné Mobembo, and CSAC ordered Perfect Télévision off air after reports about polling problems; accountability and Tshisekedi’s personal authorization were not established. [BATCH-0027-E002, BATCH-0027-E003] OLPA additionally reported that provincial media regulation was almost nonexistent and CSAC offices were under-equipped, under-resourced, and disorganized, creating conditions conducive to disinformation and ethnic or tribal hate speech. [BATCH-0006-E009] Tshisekedi’s claim that the country rose 30 places in the RSF barometer is a presidential assertion not independently substantiated here; the supplied RSF records themselves report conflicting 2023 rankings of 130th and 124th. [BATCH-0022-E006, BATCH-0002-E025, BATCH-0027-E009] Overall, formal openness and the absence of a reported nationwide internet shutdown provide limited qualifying evidence, but the documented legal, broadcast, administrative, physical, and political pressures dominate. Attribution is chiefly to state authorities, regulators, security forces, and political actors or supporters; direct presidential direction of most incidents is
